repos.title: OmniVoice: Towards Omnilingual Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Diffusion Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
OmniVoice is a zero-shot text-to-speech model covering over 600 languages. It is a single-stage non-autoregressive model: a bidirectional Transformer trained with a discrete masked diffusion objective maps text directly to 8-codebook acoustic tokens. Full-codebook random masking samples a mask for every token entry, so about 50% of tokens contribute to the loss, compared with one codebook per example in per-layer masking. The backbone is initialized from Qwen3-0.6B weights. The multilingual model trains on 581k hours from 50 open-source datasets.

On LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, it scores 0.729 SIM-o, 1.30 WER and 4.28 UTMOS, against 0.694, 1.59 and 4.28 for CosyVoice3. A bilingual variant trained on Emilia beats F5-TTS, ZipVoice and MaskGCT trained on the same corpus. Subjective SMOS is 3.80 versus 3.65 for Qwen3-TTS. On the 24-language MiniMax benchmark, Chinese character error rate is 1.008 versus 2.252 for MiniMax. Limitations: most baselines use different, larger training data; Cantonese word error rate is 17.709; and the FLEURS-102 results are not in the provided text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing zero-shot speech models cover few languages, and two-stage discrete pipelines suffer error propagation and information bottlenecks.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Method
digest_headlines.headline: Full-codebook random masking and LLM initialization form the method, trained on more than 600 languages from 581k hours of audio.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Models are compared on Chinese, English and multilingual benchmarks using speaker similarity, error rates and subjective listening scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: OmniVoice gets the lowest word error rate on LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, at 1.30, and the highest subjective similarity score, at 3.80, among compared models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that the single-stage design, masking and LLM initialization together give broad language coverage and efficient inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training datasets, inference-step and per-language results, supported languages, limitations and ethics statements.

repos.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
repos.paper_summary: StartLux-Decision is a family of 0.8B–27B decision models that output probability distributions over candidate options for typed questions. The Instant variant makes one forward pass with bidirectional attention in its full-attention layers. The AutoThink variant first makes a one-pass prediction, then generates a reasoning trace of up to 4,096 tokens only when its top probability is below 0.9, and averages the initial and post-reasoning distributions. The final training stage adds reasoning supervision and RLCD2, which uses a frozen reference model, proper-score rewards, and a soft length penalty. RLCD2 raises the share of traces that finish within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, with accuracy largely preserved. On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models beat the strongest comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4–16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink reaches 73.4. On DecisionPivot, a programmatically generated benchmark of contrast pairs, AutoThink beats its Instant counterpart by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy. Policy-aware calibration reduces confidence–accuracy gaps to within 2.7 points across 184 settings. Stated limitations include generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift, both left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Decision models need reasoning on hard cases without losing single-pass efficiency; the paper proposes two variants, RLCD2 training, and DecisionPivot.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Design and Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three-stage training gives Instant bidirectional attention and teaches AutoThink to reason only when its confidence is below 0.9.

digest_headlines.heading: RLCD2: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
digest_headlines.headline: RLCD2 rewards reasoning by the change in proper score and penalizes traces beyond a soft budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models lead comparable-scale references by 7.4–16.9 points.

digest_headlines.heading: Capability and Reliability Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Selecting among candidates makes reported confidence overconfident, and policy-aware calibration narrows the gaps across 184 settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Inference and Deployment
digest_headlines.headline: Single-pass Instant readouts on a single GPU take 24–52 ms for 256-token prompts and 31–98 ms for 1,024-token prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix documents training data sources and decontamination, policy-aware calibration proofs, and serving configuration safeguards.

repos.title: Prism: Dynamic Sparse Attention for Native 2K Joint Video-Audio Generation Model Training
repos.paper_summary: Prism is a dynamic sparse attention method for training joint video-audio generation models natively at 2K resolution. It splits the video token grid into 8×8×8 spatiotemporal macro-zones and assigns each zone a 3D block shape with 64, 128, or 256 tokens per block. The choice uses video channel-wise variance along the temporal, height, and width axes, plus audio-to-video cross-attention norms. Zones with rapid visual change and strong audio coupling get finer blocks, and repetitive backgrounds get larger ones. Per-query sparsity uses hybrid Top-k and Top-p block selection: Top-k sets a minimum coverage, and Top-p adds blocks for queries with dispersed attention. Prism inherits the MOVA DiT and replaces only video self-attention. The paper reports a 2.5× training speedup over full attention and says generation quality is higher, but the text provided does not include quality metrics. A stated limitation is that shapes are set per zone, not per token, because the Triton kernel requires contiguous 64-token tiles.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Full attention at 2K is quadratically costly and dilutes attention on informative tokens, so fixed sparse patterns fall short.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior joint video-audio models do not train natively at 2K, and trainable sparse methods use fixed block shapes.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Prism assigns each macro-zone a 3D block shape from video variance and audio coupling, then selects key blocks per query.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: On 2K-Bench, Prism beats four open-source baselines on every metric in Table 1.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Prism pairs macro-zone block shapes with hybrid selection and reports 2.5 times training speedup over full attention at 2K.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extra tables, metric definitions, the user study, ethics and limitations, and further visualizations.

repos.title: WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception from Objects to Pixels
repos.paper_summary: WeVisOne-VL is a vision-language model built on Qwen3-VL at 2B and 4B scales. It unifies object-level and pixel-level perception in one structured next-token output. Supported tasks include detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, referring segmentation, and image matting. Coordinates are emitted as dedicated tokens for values from 0 to 1000. After each predicted box, the model emits a special OBJ token. Its hidden state, the box, and multi-level ViT features feed a lightweight pixel decoder of about 9.6M parameters that predicts a mask or alpha matte. Training is three-stage SFT followed by GRPO-based mixed-task RL on samples where the SFT model is most uncertain. The data engine covers about 100M images and 3.6B box annotations, using detector proposals verified by a VLM and hard negatives for absent targets. The paper reports leading results across over 30 benchmarks, but the provided text gives no numeric scores. Stated limitations: limited general-purpose training data may reduce general capability, outputs are produced without chain-of-thought, and inference is single-turn.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current vision-language models are unreliable for fine-grained perception, so this report proposes one model covering object-level and pixel-level tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: WeVisOne-VL Data Engine
digest_headlines.headline: The data engine yields over 100 million images and approximately 3.6 billion bounding-box annotations, with verification and error-driven refinement.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Design
digest_headlines.headline: The model writes tasks as text with coordinate tokens and adds a lightweight decoder that turns object tokens into full-resolution masks.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Pipeline
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses three supervised fine-tuning stages, then reinforcement learning on uncertainty-selected samples with box-based grounding rewards.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: WeVisOne-VL-4B reaches 57.1 mean F1 on COCO and 71.3 on Dense200, above the comparable VLMs listed.

digest_headlines.heading: Qualitative Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Qualitative examples show finer instance separation, correct rejection of absent targets, and cleaner matte boundaries than the baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places the model among open-vocabulary detectors, grounded multimodal models, referring segmentation systems and promptable matting methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include possible loss of general capability, no chain-of-thought reasoning, single-turn prediction, and unclear user intent.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The model improves detection F1 and counting over comparable VLMs and surpasses the evaluated baselines on referring segmentation and matting.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training corpus sources and counts, along with hyperparameters, pixel decoder training settings and RL reward definitions.

repos.title: Optimizing the Interface Between Knowledge Graphs and LLMs for Complex Reasoning
repos.paper_summary:
Dreamify is a hyperparameter optimization framework for Cognee, a modular system that constructs knowledge graphs and retrieves context for LLMs. It uses Tree-structured Parzen Estimator to tune six parameters: chunk size, retriever type, top-k count, QA prompt, graph extraction prompt, and task preprocessing method. The authors evaluate on filtered subsets of HotPotQA, TwoWikiMultiHop, and MuSiQue, using 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset. Each experiment runs 50 trials, scoring configurations by exact match, F1, or DeepEval correctness.

Optimization yields consistent gains over default baselines. For example, HotPotQA exact match rises from 0.042 to 0.667, and F1 increases from 0.169 to 0.840. On the held-out test sets, performance generally remains above baseline but drops slightly compared to training scores; however, TwoWikiMultiHop F1 improves from 0.625 in training to 0.704 in testing. The paper notes that small evaluation sets introduce variability, and no single configuration performs best across all benchmarks, indicating that optimal settings are task-specific.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hyperparameter tuning of graph-enhanced retrieval pipelines is underexamined, though many interacting settings affect multi-hop question answering.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers retrieval-augmented pipelines, three multi-hop benchmarks, graph-based question answering, and prior optimization of such pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Automated Knowledge Graph Construction: Cognee
digest_headlines.headline: Cognee is an open-source framework whose modular pipeline and built-in evaluation let the whole system serve as an optimization objective.

digest_headlines.heading: Hyperparameter Optimization Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Dreamify tunes six Cognee parameters with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, scoring each trial by a benchmark metric averaged over questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Nine experiments pair three datasets with three metrics, each running 50 trials on 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Tuned settings beat baselines on all nine training metrics, but most hold-out scores fell below training scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Tuning gave consistent but uneven gains, and the authors call for custom benchmarks and better evaluation of graph-based systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix describes Cognee's extract-cognify-load architecture, its default pipeline stages, retriever types, and the evaluation framework.

repos.title: Kornia: an Open Source Differentiable Computer Vision Library for PyTorch
repos.paper_summary: Kornia is an open-source PyTorch library implementing differentiable computer vision operators for GPU acceleration. The package structures algorithms into modules for color conversion, feature detection, filtering, and geometry, allowing users to embed classical vision tasks directly within neural networks for backpropagation. By using PyTorch's automatic differentiation, the library computes gradients for complex functions like image warping without manual derivative implementation. The authors benchmark Sobel edge detection on 256x256 RGB images using a GTX 1080 Ti, finding that Kornia achieves the best timing performance at large batch sizes on GPU, while CPU performance lags behind optimized libraries like OpenCV. Use cases include image registration via homography optimization and multi-view depth estimation from the SceneNet dataset. Limitations include the assumption of photometric consistency in depth estimation, which restricts accuracy to small view displacements, and the fact that adversarial perturbations demonstrated in feature matching examples are not imperceptible.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Kornia is presented as a PyTorch computer vision library that runs classical image operations on GPUs as differentiable modules.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior vision libraries are mostly CPU-based, and deep learning frameworks rely on them for pre- and post-processing.

digest_headlines.heading: Kornia: Computer Vision for PyTorch.
digest_headlines.headline: Kornia is organized into PyTorch-based submodules whose operators are differentiable, batched, device-agnostic and usable across distributed systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Use cases
digest_headlines.headline: Four use cases test the library on Sobel timing, homography registration, depth estimation and adversarial matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: Classical vision tasks are reported to solve easily in PyTorch with performance similar to existing libraries.

repos.title: Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents
repos.paper_summary:
Agensh is a multi-agent harness that coordinates concurrent LLM workers without a central orchestrator. Each worker executes an asynchronous loop: gathering context, claiming sub-tasks, taking action, verifying results, and merging progress into a shared workspace. Coordination relies on three infrastructure components: a Git-based shared workspace for code integration, a message interface for peer communication, and a shared context board for reusable findings.

The paper evaluates Agensh on the five hardest ProgramBench tasks using GPT-5.6-sol (high) with a 6-hour budget. Scaling from 1 to 128 agents increases the mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%, a 49% relative improvement. On the pandoc task, scaling to 1,024 agents raises the final test-pass rate from 33.89% to 55.06%. Larger organizations also reach comparable performance levels earlier; for instance, 128 agents exceed a 30% pass rate at 30 minutes, while single agents remain below this threshold for two hours. Limitations include reliance on specific underlying models and harnesses, and the need for staggered agent activation to manage scope contention in large-scale deployments.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Agensh replaces a central orchestrator with self-organized workers, and scaling 1 to 128 agents raises mean test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Agent Organization Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Each worker repeats a five-step loop over a shared workspace, message interface and shared context, with no central orchestrator.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Multi-Agent Organization to 1,024 Agents
digest_headlines.headline: Mean test-pass rate rises with 8, 32 and 128 agents, and pandoc reaches 55.06% with 1,024 agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior harnesses keep task assignment under a fixed lead or trained orchestrator, while some tools coordinate workers through shared state.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agent count is proposed as a new scaling dimension, though every reported run uses one agent model.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the worker prompt, the event-driven runtime, the experiment configuration and the staggered agent launch schedule.

repos.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
repos.paper_summary: SWE-bench is an evaluation benchmark of 2294 software engineering tasks drawn from GitHub issues and their merged pull requests across 12 popular Python repositories. A model receives an issue text and a codebase snapshot and must produce a patch that makes the repository's fail-to-pass tests pass without breaking existing tests. Tasks were collected with a 33-stage pipeline that filters PRs for issue resolution, test changes, and successful execution. The authors also release SWE-bench Lite, a 300-instance subset, a training set (SWE-bench-train, about 19,000 instances from 37 other repositories), and two fine-tuned CodeLlama-Python models, SWE-Llama 7b and 13b, trained with LoRA on attention weights. Context is selected with BM25 retrieval or with oracle files from the reference patch. The best model, Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval, resolves 1.96% of tasks; with oracle retrieval it resolves 4.8%. Performance falls as context length grows. The authors note that the benchmark covers only Python, and that execution-based tests do not capture code efficiency, readability, or comprehensiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks are saturated, so the authors propose SWE-bench, which draws tasks from real GitHub issues.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench pairs GitHub issues with merged pull requests and grades patches by running the repository's tests.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-Llama: Fine-tuning CodeLlama for SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning CodeLlama-Python on issue-patch pairs produces SWE-Llama, open models that edit repositories.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Each model gets context from sparse retrieval or from oracle files that the reference patch edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Claude 2 is the best model at 1.96% resolved, and resolution falls as the total context length grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier benchmarks use narrow tasks or single functions, which SWE-bench extends to multi-file repository edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include Python-only tasks, simple baselines, and execution tests that miss readability and efficiency.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench uses public repositories with licenses permitting software use, and involves no human subjects or GitHub user data.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, all 2294 task instances, and technical details for collection and evaluation are provided for reproduction.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers construction, field definitions, execution-based validation, dataset statistics, and case studies of model patches.

repos.title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
repos.paper_summary: HairDeck generates the stylized hair cards of a character and the spring-bone chains that animate them, from a point cloud or a single image. Each card is one continuous token from a card VAE, and a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding denoises all card tokens of a hairstyle together with flow matching; an existence flag on each token sets the card count. A second set DiT generates the spring-bone chains from the card tokens. Training uses 36,440 CHARM hairstyles from VRoid characters, plus synthetic style augmentation and renders restyled by an image-editing model. On CHARM's 100-hairstyle test set, Chamfer distance drops from 0.0117 (CHARM) to 0.0066 and orientation error from 40.0° to 16.8°, at 1.01 s per hairstyle against 33.7 s for CHARM. On 76 rendered single-image test characters, CD is 0.0089 against 0.0139 to 0.0186 for baselines, with a 3.5% failure rate against 13.2% to 34.2%. The paper states that very short hair and alpha-textured realistic cards are outside the training data, and that no textures are generated.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing generators do not output the artist-placed hair cards of stylized characters, so HairDeck generates each card as one token.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers strand hair, realistic cards, stylized characters and set generation, but CHARM is the only prior stylized card generator.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each card is encoded as one continuous token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all tokens together without positional embedding.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On CHARM's test set HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance from 0.0117 to 0.0066 and orientation error from 40.0° to 16.8°, taking 1.01 s.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: HairDeck outputs card geometry without textures and learns only from stylized VRoid hairstyles, so short hair and realistic cards fall outside it.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation settings, appearance augmentation, chain metrics, export, baseline details, and additional comparisons and results.

repos.title: Constraint Breeds Generalization: Temporal Dynamics as an Inductive Bias
repos.paper_summary: This paper argues that dissipative temporal dynamics, meaning phase-space contraction, act as an inductive bias that improves generalization in spiking neural networks (SNNs). Static features are converted into time series by a Duffing oscillator whose parameter δ sets the dynamics as expansive (δ<0), transition (δ≈0 to 2), or dissipative. Leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with leak β provide an architecture-level variant. On handwritten digits (64 features, 10 classes), SNNs trained in the transition regime generalize across a 12×12 matrix of encodings, while expansive-trained networks fail outside their training encoding. On CIFAR-10 patches, the transition regime yields localized, oriented receptive fields (structure score 0.206, versus 0.0541 for the best alternative in Table 1). Experiment 3 reports zero-shot transfer to unseen physical environments in reinforcement learning that beats baseline architectures. Limitations include fixed oscillator and fixed β parameters, and generality is checked only on a few alternative dynamical systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hypothesizes that dissipative temporal dynamics act as an inductive bias for generalization, tested at representational, structural, and behavioral levels.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Controls phase-space contraction through a single oscillator parameter δ for static inputs and neuron leak β for temporal inputs.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Argues the transition regime trades fit for stability; the authors flag fixed parameters and untested regime generality as limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Concludes that dissipative dynamics are an inductive bias, so generalization may depend on dynamical regime as much as on scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists oscillator equations and parameters, a dynamical indicator table, experiment details, Bayesian bound and gradient analyses, and extra figures.
